rationale: The hypothesis posits a distinct genotype-phenotype correlation in Stolerman neurodevelopmental syndrome (KDM6B-related disorder), suggesting that catalytic JmjC missense variants result in more severe intellectual disability, higher seizure penetrance, and pronounced structural anomalies compared to truncating variants. However, the definitive systematic cohort study evaluating the clinical and molecular spectrum of KDM6B (Rots et al., 2023) explicitly found no genotype-phenotype correlation explaining clinical severity or phenotypic manifestations between variant types (truncating vs. missense/in-frame indels). While missense mutations indeed cluster around the catalytic JmjC/Zn-finger domains, empirical cohort evaluations refute the existence of the hypothesized distinct, more severe clinical trajectory.

evidence.text: A comprehensive study characterizing the clinical and molecular spectrum of KDM6B-related disorder analyzed truncating variants as well as 11 missense/in-frame indels in or near the enzymatic JmjC or Zn-containing domains and explicitly concluded that there was no genotype-phenotype correlation observed.

new_directions.question_text: Do specific missense variants in the catalytic iron-binding or alpha-ketoglutarate-binding residues of the JmjC domain exert dominant-negative vs. pure loss-of-function enzymatic effects in functional assays?
new_directions.rationale: Although gross clinical classification shows no broad genotype-phenotype correlation, functional biochemical profiling of specific JmjC active site substitutions may explain outlier clinical presentations such as structural brain heterotopias.
